summary: A square brick light on Mark Island at the western entrance to the Deer Island Thorofare, off Stonington, Maine. Owned by the Island Heritage Trust since 1998.

structures.note: Square brick tower joined to a seven-room frame dwelling by a brick workroom. The dwelling burned in 1958; the tower was saved.

access.note: USLHS: not open to the public. LighthouseFriends: grounds open and tower closed; best viewed from the water. Owned by the Island Heritage Trust.

events.note: Congress appropriated the requested money in August 1856; Mark Island bought from David and Mercy Thurlow that December for $175.
Construction of the square brick tower began in the summer of 1857 (LighthouseFriends). USLHS gives 1857 as the station's year established.
Fixed white light first shown at sunset, 1 March 1858. USLHS gives 1858 as the year the tower was established.
Keeper's dwelling clapboarded and painted white.
About 175 trees cut to make the light visible from all approaches.
Bell struck by machinery, a double blow every fifteen seconds, in a frame tower 75 feet northwest of the light; began 15 October 1884.
Fog-signal tests run at Deer Island Thoroughfare on 2 June 1894; the observer tracked the limit of audibility of the bell.
An oil house and a fuel house built.
New beam for the bell; striker moved outside the bell.
Keeper Allen C. Holt towed the disabled steamer Minnehaha to a place of safety on 13 May 1917.
Station automated; the Coast Guard decided to automate rather than rebuild the dwelling.
Battery charger exploded in the dwelling's basement on 10 September 1958; the dwelling was a total loss, and the brick tower was saved.
A continuously sounded horn replaced the fog bell; outbuildings torn down; a modern optic replaced the Fresnel lens.
Horn's power reduced and the horn relocated in July 1959 after neighbours complained.
Ownership passed to the Island Heritage Trust, 1998 (IHT); announced late 1997 (LighthouseFriends).

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends says the light was first shown at sunset on 1 March 1858, and the USLHS gives 1858 for the tower. The record's 1857 is the year the station was established and construction began. Human review: if the record is meant to hold the year of station establishment, leave it.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The USLHS gives 1857 for the station's establishment and 1858 for the tower. LighthouseFriends says construction began in 1857 and the light was first shown on 1 March 1858. Wikipedia (not cited) says the tower was built in 1857. The story uses both dates.
LighthouseFriends dates John E. Purington's service from 1912; the USLHS roster lists 1914 to 1916. The story gives the roster's span and notes LighthouseFriends' 1912.
LighthouseFriends dates the fire to 10 September 1958. Wikipedia's lead (not cited) says 1959. The story uses 1958.
LighthouseFriends says the Maine Lights Program transferred 35 lighthouses; the Trust's page says 36. The story gives both numbers, with the source for each.

The USLHS lists the station as not open to the public. LighthouseFriends says the grounds are open and the tower closed. The story gives both and no longer tells visitors to check with the Trust, which the Trust's page does not say.
The USLHS record lists a fog-signal building constructed in 1908; LighthouseFriends describes the bell from 1884 and a horn from 1958. Not resolved.

notes_for_editor: Confidence is medium: the construction and keeper details rest mainly on LighthouseFriends, a copyrighted community site; facts are paraphrased and only one short phrase is quoted. The Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1917 OCR reads 'Minnehahn'; the name is given as Minnehaha (LighthouseFriends). Commissioner's report 1918 mentions 'Mark Island, West Penobscot Bay' (Islesboro area). That is a different light and was not used. The Light-House Board's FY1894 page for the fog-signal test is cited by scan page 726; the printed page was not confirmed. The 1895 item (225) is cited by scan page. LighthouseFriends prints the keeper as 'Alva Robinson' in Mitchell's account; the roster reads 'Alvah Robinson', and the roster spelling is used. Mitchell's account is undated in the excerpt LighthouseFriends prints; the story says so. Ralph Stanley Andrews (keeper 1945 to 1948) is named only as the former keeper at the 1998 celebration, per LighthouseFriends; his medical detail is not used. Roster lines for keepers after about 1960 (Kwapiszewski, Friend, McPherson, Hines) are in the JSON as printed and are not named in the story. Not read: the USCG Historian's archived page for this light (web.archive.org returned 404); the New England Lighthouses history by D'Entremont (copyrighted, facts only); Marnie Reed Crowell's Mark Island Light. An Ellsworth American notice of 1906 mentions a shoal near the light in Deer Island Thoroughfare; it was not used. Position: the record's OSM point (44.134369 N, 68.703253 W) and the USLHS point (44 08 N, 68 42.2 W) differ by about 0.4 km; no correction proposed.
